title: Place Value Grade 5 Large Numbers: Read, Write & Expand to Crores + Free Quiz
meta_title: Place Value Grade 5 Large Numbers (Crores) + Quiz
meta_desc: Master place value grade 5 large numbers: read and write to crores and millions, Indian vs international commas, and expanded form, plus a free quiz.
excerpt: Your child could add and subtract lakhs in Grade 4. Grade 5 pushes past that — to crores, to millions, and to the moment they finally see why the commas fall where they do. Here is how to teach it, with a quick quiz to check.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Write 3450672 on a board and ask a Grade 5 class to read it aloud. Half will start confidently — ‘three million…’ — then trail off, unsure where the words go. The other half will count digits on their fingers. This stumble is the whole of place value grade 5 large numbers in one moment: the digits are known, but the structure that turns them into ‘thirty-four lakh fifty thousand six hundred seventy-two’ is not yet automatic. Fixing that structure is the single most useful thing you can do this year.

By the end of Grade 4 a child can usually handle numbers up to lakhs. Grade 5 stretches that in two directions at once: bigger numbers (crores, and their international cousin millions) and a sharper grasp of what each digit is actually worth. The commas are the key, and this is where most confusion hides.

Why place value for large numbers trips up Grade 5

The number itself does not change. What changes is how we group its digits, and India teaches two grouping systems side by side. In the Indian system we group as 3, then 2, then 2: 34,50,672. In the international system we group in threes throughout: 3,450,672. Same number, different commas, different names. A child who has only ever seen one system freezes when a textbook, a bank statement, and a news headline each use a different one.

So the first job is not drilling — it is making the two systems sit next to each other until the difference stops being scary.

The two place-value charts, side by side

I put both charts on one sheet and never separate them. Reading top to bottom, notice that the first difference appears only above the thousands.

Indian systemValueInternational systemValue
Ones1Ones1
Tens10Tens10
Hundreds100Hundreds100
Thousands1,000Thousands1,000
Ten thousands10,000Ten thousands10,000
Lakhs1,00,000Hundred thousands100,000
Ten lakhs10,00,000Millions1,000,000
Crores1,00,00,000Ten millions10,000,000

The pattern to point out: below a thousand, the two systems are identical. Above it, India inserts a comma every two digits while the international system keeps going in threes. One lakh is a hundred thousand; one crore is ten million. Say those two equalities out loud until they feel obvious — they are the bridge between the columns.

Reading and writing to crores (Indian system)

Here is the routine that works. Start from the right and place commas by the Indian rule — first after three digits, then after every two. Take 34506720. From the right: 34506720 becomes 3,45,06,720. Now read left to right in chunks: 3 crore, 45 lakh, 06 thousand, 720. So ‘three crore forty-five lakh six thousand seven hundred twenty.’

The common mistake with the comma

Children who learned the international ‘every three digits’ rule in a video will often write 3,450,6720 and get lost. Insist on the Indian rhythm — three, then two, then two — when the number is in the Indian system. Mixing the two rules in one number is the error I correct most often.

The value of each digit — not just its name

A digit’s place tells you what it is worth, and this is where real understanding lives. In 3,45,06,720 the digit 5 is not just ‘a five’ — it sits in the lakhs place, so it is worth 5,00,000. The 4 beside it is in ten lakhs, worth 40,00,000. Ask a child ‘what is this digit worth?’ rather than ‘what place is this digit in?’ The first question is harder and far more useful.

  • Face value is the digit itself — the 5 is just 5.
  • Place value is the digit multiplied by its place — the 5 in the lakhs column is worth 5,00,000.
  • The two are equal only in the ones place, which is a nice check.

Expanded form pulls it all together

Expanded form is where place value stops being a chart and becomes a habit. Writing a number as the sum of the value of each digit forces a child to name every place. For 3,45,06,720:

  • 3,00,00,000 + 40,00,000 + 5,00,000 + 0 + 6,000 + 7,00 + 20
  • Or, more honestly, drop the zero terms: 3,00,00,000 + 40,00,000 + 5,00,000 + 6,000 + 700 + 20.

One caveat I always add: the zero in the ten-thousands place is not decoration. Remove it and the number collapses from three-crore-something to three-lakh-something. Zeros hold places open. A child who respects zeros rarely misplaces a comma.

A realistic weekly routine

Ten minutes a day beats a marathon on Sunday. Two days on reading numbers aloud from both systems, two days on writing dictated numbers with correct commas, and one day on expanded form and digit values. On the weekend, mix them — give a number and ask for its Indian reading, its international reading, and the value of one chosen digit. That switching is where fluency shows.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a free eight-question quiz on exactly this — reading to crores, Indian versus international commas, digit values, and expanded form. Let your child try it and read the explanations together for anything they miss. When they are ready for longer written practice, the printable worksheet at the end has graded questions with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 5 Place Value: Large Numbers Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on reading and writing large numbers, Indian and international commas, digit values and expanded form. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 5 place value of large numbers to crores and millions

questions.q: How is 3450672 written with commas in the Indian system?
questions.explanation: Indian grouping is three digits from the right, then two, then two: 34,50,672 — thirty-four lakh fifty thousand six hundred seventy-two.

questions.q: In the number 5,60,842 what is the value of the digit 6?
questions.explanation: The 6 sits in the ten-thousands place, so its value is 6 × 10,000 = 60,000.

questions.q: One crore is the same as how many in the international system?
questions.explanation: 1 crore = 1,00,00,000 = 10,000,000, which reads as ten million.

questions.q: How is 2,300,000 (international) written in the Indian system?
questions.explanation: 2,300,000 is twenty-three lakh, written 23,00,000 with commas after three then two digits.

questions.q: What is the expanded form of 47,205?
questions.explanation: Each digit times its place: 40,000 + 7,000 + 200 + 0 + 5. The tens digit is 0, so it contributes nothing.

questions.q: Which number is 'six crore five lakh three thousand twenty'?
questions.explanation: Six crore = 6, five lakh = 05, three thousand = 03,020. Putting them together gives 6,05,03,020.

questions.q: In 8,04,916 the digit 0 is in which place?
questions.explanation: Reading right to left: 6 ones, 1 ten, 9 hundred, 4 thousand, 0 ten-thousand, 8 lakh. The 0 holds the ten-thousands place open.
1 lakh = 1,00,000 = 100,000, which is one hundred thousand in the international system.

faq.q: What place values should a Grade 5 child know?
faq.a: Up to crores in the Indian system (ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, lakhs, ten lakhs, crores) and up to ten millions in the international system. They should also read and write numbers in both, place commas correctly, and give the value of any digit.

faq.q: What is the difference between the Indian and international comma systems?
faq.a: Both are identical up to thousands. Above that, the Indian system groups in twos (34,50,672) while the international system groups in threes (3,450,672). One lakh equals one hundred thousand, and one crore equals ten million.

faq.q: How is face value different from place value?
faq.a: Face value is just the digit itself — the 7 in 7,45,000 has a face value of 7. Place value is the digit multiplied by its position, so that same 7 in the lakhs place has a place value of 7,00,000. They match only in the ones place.

faq.q: Why does my child keep putting commas in the wrong place?
faq.a: Usually because they mix the two systems — applying the international ‘every three digits’ rule to an Indian number. Teach one rhythm at a time: for the Indian system, three digits from the right, then twos.
